titleText.es: Quiero decir que la parte en blanco y negro iba hacia atrás, pero apenas aportaba nada a la historia.
titleText.en: I mean, the black-and-white part was going backward, but it contributed almost nothing to the story.

regions.labelEs: SOY MALO PARA LAS DESPEDIDAS. A UN CIERTO NIVEL NUNCA PIENSO QUE SEAN REALES.

applications.explanationEn: Soy identifies the speaker, malo states the lack of skill or comfort, para introduces the situation, and despedidas fills that situation slot.
The complete fixed phrase introduces one particular layer at which the speaker's next statement feels true.
Nunca makes the belief negative, pienso names the belief, que introduces its content, and sean uses the doubted-idea form rather than ordinary son.

regions.labelEs: ME HACEN PENSAR EN EL MERLÍN DE T. H. WHITE

applications.explanationEn: Me is the affected person, hacen supplies the causing action, and pensar en introduces the person or thing brought to mind.

regions.labelEs: VIVÍA HACIA ATRÁS, RECORDANDO EL FUTURO PERO NO EL PASADO. PARA ÉL, LAS DESPEDIDAS FINALES NO SIGNIFICABAN NADA, MIENTRAS QUE LOS PRIMEROS SALUDOS ERAN DOLOROSOS Y AGRIDULCES.

applications.explanationEn: Hacia establishes a direction and atrás specifies that the direction is backward.
Recordando uses the -ando action form to add the remembering that accompanies the way he lived.
The two-word connector introduces the contrasting treatment of first greetings.

regions.labelEs: OH. ENTONCES, CON LOS AÑOS OLVIDARÍA A TODOS SUS AMIGOS.

applications.explanationEn: The complete time expression frames the forgetting as a gradual change over passing years.
Olvidaría keeps the full verb olvidar and adds -ía to express what he would do under the imagined time direction.
Debió and de mark a past inference, while sentirse is the unchanged action whose truth the speaker is inferring.
Sentirse introduces a person's emotional state, and solo supplies the masculine singular description of that state.

regions.labelEs: SÍ. TERMINÓ APOLTRONÁNDOSE EN CASA VIENDO DVDs TODO EL DÍA. LO MEJOR FUE EL DÍA QUE ALQUILÓ “MEMENTO”...

applications.explanationEn: Terminó introduces the eventual outcome, and apoltronándose uses the -ando form to name the action that became that outcome.
Viendo uses the irregular -iendo action form to add the activity that accompanies being at home.
Todo agrees with the masculine noun día, and the three-word expression gives the activity's duration.
Neutral lo turns mejor into an unnamed best aspect or event rather than describing a masculine noun.
El día names the time, que links it to an event, and alquiló supplies that event's completed action.

cards.promptEs: ser malo/a para + nombre o infinitivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is bad at an activity or situation?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ser, malo or mala, para, and then the activity or situation.
cards.noteEn: Malo changes to mala for a feminine subject. The final slot can be a noun or an unchanged action verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: I am bad at mathematics.

cards.answerEn: bad at; not skilled at (masculine singular)
cards.noteEn: With ser and para, malo describes a person as not skilled or comfortable with an activity or situation.

example.en: I am bad at remembering names.

cards.answerEn: at; with (introducing what someone is good or bad at)
cards.noteEn: After bueno or malo, para can introduce the activity or situation in which someone is skilled or unskilled.

example.en: She is good at languages.

cards.noteEn: Spanish uses a before nivel when describing the level or layer at which something is true.

example.es: A otro nivel, el problema cambia.
example.en: At another level, the problem changes.

cards.questionEn: How do you qualify a statement by saying it is true at some level?
cards.noteEn: The phrase introduces one layer, degree, or way of looking at a situation. It often softens or limits the claim that follows.

example.es: A un cierto nivel, estoy de acuerdo.
example.en: At some level, I agree.

cards.questionEn: What verb form usually follows a negative belief such as “I do not think that…”?
cards.answerEn: After the negative belief and que, use the form that presents the idea as doubted rather than asserted as fact.
cards.noteEn: For many verbs, this form has a changed ending: habla becomes hable, and comen becomes coman. A positive belief normally uses the ordinary fact-stating form instead.

example.es: No creo que Ana esté aquí.
example.en: I do not think Ana is here.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: they are; may be (subjunctive form of ser)
cards.noteEn: Sean is used for plural subjects when the speaker is not presenting their being as a plain fact, for example after doubt or a negative belief.

example.en: I do not think they are the same.

cards.promptEs: hacer pensar en + persona o cosa
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something reminds someone of another person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use hacer, the person affected, pensar en, and then what comes to mind.
cards.noteEn: The form of hacer matches the thing causing the association. The person can appear as me, te, le, nos, or another object expression.

example.es: Esta canción me hace pensar en casa.
example.en: This song makes me think of home.

cards.noteEn: Hacen is the plural present form of hacer. Before another action verb, it can mean that something causes a person to do or experience that action.

example.en: Those photos make me smile.

cards.noteEn: Pensar en means to think of or think about someone or something.

example.en: I think about my family.

cards.promptEs: Merlín · T. H. White · vida hacia atrás
cards.answerEn: references T. H. White's Merlin, who experiences time backward
cards.noteEn: In The Once and Future King, T. H. White portrays Merlin as living backward through time. He knows events that are still in other people's future while his own past becomes their future.
Ah can be used as a brief questioning response when someone has not understood or expects an explanation.

example.en: “The meeting changed locations.” “Huh?”

cards.answerEn: he lived; he used to live
cards.noteEn: Vivía describes an ongoing or habitual situation in the past.

example.en: I used to live near the sea.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that movement, direction, or progress goes backward?
cards.noteEn: Hacia supplies the direction and atrás points toward the back or reverse. The phrase can describe physical movement or an abstract process.

example.en: The video is going backward.

cards.noteEn: Recordando is the -ando form of recordar and presents the remembering as an action in progress or accompanying another action.

example.en: She walked while remembering the trip.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

example.en: She came in running.

cards.noteEn: The written accent distinguishes the pronoun él from the article el, which means “the.”

example.en: The book is for him.

cards.noteEn: Significaban describes an ongoing or general meaning in the past.

example.en: Those signs meant danger.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

example.en: I don’t see anything.

cards.questionEn: How do you contrast two facts with “whereas” or “while”?
cards.answerEn: Use mientras que before the contrasting fact.
cards.noteEn: This use compares two different situations. It is different from plain mientras when that word only means that two actions happen at the same time.

example.es: Ella madruga, mientras que yo trabajo de noche.
example.en: She gets up early, whereas I work at night.

cards.noteEn: Agridulce literally combines agrio, “sour,” and dulce, “sweet,” and can describe mixed happy and sad feelings.

example.en: The farewell left bittersweet memories.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something changes gradually as years pass?
cards.noteEn: The expression means “over the years” or “with the passing of time,” not merely that something is accompanied by years.

example.es: Con los años, la ciudad cambió.
example.en: Over the years, the city changed.

cards.noteEn: Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.noteEn: Olvidaría combines the dictionary form olvidar with the conditional ending -ía.

example.es: Sin una nota, olvidaría la cita.
example.en: Without a note, she would forget the appointment.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

example.en: We would travel by train.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

example.en: I see Marta.

cards.answerEn: he must have; he probably did
cards.noteEn: With de and an action verb, debió presents a conclusion about what was probably true in the past, not a duty someone had to perform.

example.en: He must have missed the train.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something must be true because the evidence makes it likely?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern makes an inference or educated guess. Without de, deber plus an action verb more often expresses a duty or what someone should do.

example.en: They must be at home.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks an inference after deber
cards.noteEn: In deber de plus an action verb, de helps mark a guess or conclusion about what is likely true.

example.en: She must be tired.

cards.answerEn: to feel; to find oneself feeling
cards.noteEn: Sentirse is sentir with the pronominal ending se. It is followed by a description of someone's physical or emotional state.

example.es: Después del viaje, se sintió cansado.
example.en: After the trip, he felt tired.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe how a person feels?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of sentirse followed by a describing word.
cards.noteEn: The describing word normally changes to agree with the person: cansado for a man, cansada for a woman, and plural forms for more than one person.

example.en: We feel calm.

cards.noteEn: When solo describes a masculine person's state, it means alone or lonely rather than “only.” The feminine form is sola.

example.es: Se sintió solo en la ciudad nueva.
example.en: He felt lonely in the new city.

cards.noteEn: Before an -ando or -iendo action form, terminó describes the final outcome of a process or series of events.

example.en: She ended up living in Madrid.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone eventually ended up doing something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of terminar followed by the action form ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: The pattern emphasizes the eventual outcome, often after an unexpected process. It does not simply say that the person finished the action.

example.en: We ended up talking all night.

cards.answerEn: settling lazily into an armchair; lounging
cards.noteEn: Apoltronándose comes from apoltronarse, a vivid verb for making oneself comfortable and inactive, as if sinking into an armchair.

example.es: Pasó la tarde apoltronándose frente al televisor.
example.en: He spent the afternoon lounging in front of the television.

cards.noteEn: Viendo is the irregular -iendo form of ver.

example.en: I am watching a film.

cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly keeps the international abbreviation DVD and adds a written plural s in informal use.

example.es: Guardó los DVDs en una caja.
example.en: She kept the DVDs in a box.

cards.promptEs: todo/toda + el/la + período de tiempo singular
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something continues for an entire day, night, week, or similar period?
cards.answerEn: Use todo or toda, then the matching singular article el or la, then the time period.
cards.noteEn: Todo and the article match the time noun: todo el día, toda la noche, toda la semana. This pattern covers the whole named period. Plural forms such as todos los años usually mean “every year” and are a separate frequency pattern.

example.en: It rained all day.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to “the best thing” or “the best part” without naming a noun?
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns mejor into an abstract idea. The phrase does not refer to a masculine noun; it means whatever aspect is best.

example.en: The best thing is to rest.

cards.noteEn: With el, la, lo, los, or las, mejor usually means “best.” Without one of those words, it often means “better.”

example.en: This is the best option.

cards.answerEn: was (a completed past instance of ser)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a named time to the event that happened then?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the time noun, then give the event as a clause.
cards.noteEn: After a time expression such as el día or el año, que can work like English “when.” The Spanish connector remains que.

example.es: Recuerdo el día que nos conocimos.
example.en: I remember the day when we met.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Alquiló is a completed-past form of alquilar. The final accent marks the stressed last syllable.

example.en: He rented a bicycle yesterday.

cards.answerEn: references Memento, a film whose color scenes run in reverse chronological order
cards.noteEn: Christopher Nolan's Memento follows a man with severe short-term memory loss. One sequence of scenes moves backward in time, so viewers repeatedly learn what happened just before the scene they have seen.
As a one-word reaction, elemental says that a conclusion is basic or easy to deduce.

example.en: The answer is elementary.
